clue.text: The bondsman's two hundred and fifty years of — toil shall be sunk " (Abraham Lincoln)

definitions.text: The bondsman's two hundred and fifty years of — toil shall be sunk " (Abraham Lincoln)

parts.words: The bondsman's two hundred and fifty years of — toil shall be sunk " (Abraham Lincoln)
parts.note: a gap-fill quotation from Lincoln's Second Inaugural Address: the missing adjective describes slave labour never paid for

explanation.surface: A line from Lincoln about the long, unpaid labour of enslaved people.
explanation.walkthrough: Lincoln's Second Inaugural (1865) speaks of 'all the wealth piled by the bondsman's two hundred and fifty years of unrequited toil'; the solver supplies the missing word.
explanation.definitionFit: Toil that is never repaid or rewarded is unreturned labour, the sense Lincoln gives the word.

clue.text: Toward a Biblical version

parts.note: the clue asks for the King James Bible's way of saying 'to' or 'towards'

explanation.definitionFit: The archaic preposition meaning 'to' appears throughout the Authorised Version, as in 'unto us a child is born'.

clue.text: They pay late, quoth the Raven

definitions.text: They pay late, quoth the Raven

parts.words: They pay late, quoth the Raven
parts.note: the Raven is the novelist Simon Raven, whose 1964 novel title says which people pay late

explanation.surface: Poe's bird delivering a gloomy verdict on bad debtors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quoth the Raven' points at Poe's poem, but the Raven is Simon Raven, whose novel 'The Rich Pay Late' opens his Alms for Oblivion sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: Simon Raven's novel title names the wealthy as the late payers.

clue.text: He wrote on green baize, they say

definitions.text: He wrote on green baize, they say

parts.words: He wrote on green baize, they say
parts.note: the writer signed himself with the letter Q, which sounds like a cue, the stick used on a green baize billiard table

explanation.surface: A gambler or snooker player scribbling on the card table.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Arthur Quiller-Couch wrote under the pen name 'Q'; said out loud, Q is 'cue', the snooker or billiards stick that lies on the green baize.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cornish man of letters and Oxford Book of English Verse editor used the single-letter pseudonym Q.

clue.text: Manner of expression used by fool, mostly, at start of manuscript

indicators.note: mostly means the word for fool loses its final letter

parts.note: an idiot is a fool

indicators.note: start of means only the opening letter of manuscript is taken

explanation.surface: A writer's way of phrasing things shows up in the opening of a draft by a dunce.
explanation.definitionFit: A characteristic turn of phrase in a language or writer is a manner of expression.

clue.text: What Graham Greene apparently expected his lighter novels to do

definitions.text: What Graham Greene apparently expected his lighter novels to do

parts.words: What Graham Greene apparently expected his lighter novels to do
parts.note: Greene labelled his thrillers ..., so the clue asks for the verb behind that label

explanation.walkthrough: Greene divided his fiction into serious 'novels' and lighter 'entertainments' such as Stamboul Train; the verb is drawn from that label.
explanation.definitionFit: Books meant to amuse and divert readers are expected to amuse them, the verb behind Greene's category.

clue.text: Requisite attribute of time, according to Huxley

definitions.text: Requisite attribute of time, according to Huxley

parts.words: Requisite attribute of time, according to Huxley
parts.note: refers to Aldous Huxley's novel 'Time Must Have a ...', whose title names what time must have

explanation.definitionFit: Huxley's title, borrowed from Henry IV Part 1, says time must have an end or halt.

clue.text: "Milton has ennobled (the sonnet) in our tongue, and has —d it in (Italian)" (W. S. Landor)

definitions.text: "Milton has ennobled (the sonnet) in our tongue, and has —d it in (Italian)" (W. S. Landor)

parts.words: "Milton has ennobled (the sonnet) in our tongue, and has —d it in (Italian)" (W. S. Landor)
parts.note: a gap-fill quotation from Landor: the missing verb is the opposite of ennobled, making the sonnet petty

explanation.surface: Landor contrasting Milton's lofty English sonnets with his lesser Italian ones.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb is the antonym of 'ennobled': to make something petty or of little worth.

clue.text: Attorney supplying drink to builder

parts.note: perry is a drink made from fermented pears
a mason is a builder in stone

explanation.surface: A lawyer handing a drink to a construction worker.
explanation.definitionFit: Erle Stanley Gardner's fictional defence lawyer is the best-known attorney of crime fiction.

clue.text: They like to keep in touch with art

definitions.text: They like to keep in touch with art

parts.words: They like to keep in touch with art
parts.note: 'keep in touch' is read literally: followers of Marinetti's art of touch, which works on the sense of feeling

explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep in touch' sounds like staying in contact; it means art made to be felt with the hands, the Tactilism Marinetti launched in 1921.
explanation.definitionFit: Exponents of Tactilism, the Futurist movement of art appreciated by feeling, are devotees of art through touch.

clue.text: Fisher boy was born such in Waterhouse book

definitions.text: Fisher boy was born such in Waterhouse book

parts.words: Fisher boy was born such in Waterhouse book
parts.note: Billy Fisher is the hero of Keith Waterhouse's novel, a habitual fantasist whose nickname gives the title

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fisher boy' looks like a young angler; it is Billy Fisher of Keith Waterhouse's 'Billy Liar' (1959), a born teller of tall tales.
explanation.definitionFit: Billy Fisher compulsively invents stories, so he is a natural fibber, as the novel's title says.

clue.text: Militant republicans presumably not expected to fill the breeches

definitions.text: Militant republicans presumably not expected to fill the breeches

parts.words: Militant republicans presumably not expected to fill the breeches
parts.note: the French name of these revolutionaries literally means 'without knee-breeches', since they wore trousers

explanation.walkthrough: The radical working-class revolutionaries of 1790s Paris wore long trousers rather than the aristocrat's culottes, hence the name 'without breeches'.
explanation.definitionFit: The radical Parisian revolutionaries took their name from not wearing the knee-breeches of the upper classes.

clue.text: Ancient death of Scott's fanatic fellow-traveller

parts.note: ancient means old
mortality means death

explanation.surface: An aged corpse in Walter Scott keeping company with a zealot.
explanation.walkthrough: In Scott's novel the title character is an old Covenanter who wanders Scotland recutting the gravestones of fellow believers, a zealous companion of their cause.
explanation.definitionFit: Scott's title figure is a devout Covenanter who travels about restoring martyrs' tombs, a zealous follower of their cause.

clue.text: Strange mania a girl reveals for reader's notes

indicators.note: strange signals that the following letters are rearranged into an odd new order

explanation.surface: A peculiar obsession shown by a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Notes written in the margins of a book by the person reading it are its marginal jottings.

clue.text: Lord Chancellor's was spontaneous

parts.note: the 'Lord Chancellor' is Krook, the rag-and-bone dealer so nicknamed in Dickens's Bleak House, who bursts into flame

explanation.walkthrough: Not a real Lord Chancellor: Krook in Bleak House is nicknamed 'the Lord Chancellor' and dies by spontaneous burning.
explanation.definitionFit: Krook's death in Bleak House is the famous literary case of a body igniting by itself.

clue.text: Fourteen excluded books

parts.note: the fourteen books printed between the Testaments in the King James Bible but left out of the Hebrew canon

explanation.definitionFit: These fourteen texts were excluded from the Protestant biblical canon as of doubtful authority.

clue.text: Poor pet in daze from nitpick

indicators.note: poor signals the following letters are in bad shape and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A sad pet, dazed after being picked at for nits.
explanation.definitionFit: To quibble over trivial points of detail is to behave like a fussy stickler.

clue.text: General and dictator, some sort of consul, later

indicators.note: some sort of means that a part of the following words is taken, running across them

explanation.surface: A Roman general who became dictator and later held some sort of consulship.
explanation.walkthrough: The Roman frame invites a historical guess, but the name runs across 'consul, later'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucius Cornelius Sulla was a Roman general who made himself dictator in 82 BC.

clue.text: Blind Venetian old boy is on dangerous ground, coming back

indicators.note: coming back means the combined letters are read in reverse

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil
a bog is treacherous marshy ground

explanation.surface: A blind old man in Venice back on treacherous terrain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming back' turns OBBOG round. Old Gobbo in The Merchant of Venice is 'sand-blind'.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Gobbo, Launcelot's father in The Merchant of Venice, is nearly blind and fails to recognise his son.

clue.text: Italian Renaissance man, creator of La Gioconda

definitions.text: Italian Renaissance man, creator of La Gioconda

parts.words: Italian Renaissance man, creator of La Gioconda
parts.note: points not to Leonardo but to the poet-playwright-aviator who wrote a tragedy named La Gioconda in 1898

explanation.walkthrough: 'Renaissance man' and 'La Gioconda' scream Leonardo, but this is the 1898 play by the poet, soldier and aviator Gabriele D'Annunzio, a polymath in the broad sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Gabriele D'Annunzio was an Italian poet, dramatist, novelist and airman whose play was titled La Gioconda.

clue.text: Yeats subject, not a reincarnation of Hardy NCO

definitions.meaning: a poem by W. B. Yeats about Maud Gonne, comparing her to Helen

definitions.text: not a reincarnation of Hardy NCO
definitions.meaning: Sergeant Troy in Hardy's Far from the Madding Crowd is the NCO; no second one means no reincarnation

explanation.surface: Yeats on whether a Hardy soldier lives again.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hardy NCO is Sergeant Frank Troy of Far from the Madding Crowd; Yeats's poem title, meant of the city, reads as 'no second sergeant'.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeats's poem title, about the city Helen doomed, also reads as denying a second coming of Hardy's sergeant.

clue.text: Thomas Fuller maintained it in print

definitions.text: Thomas Fuller maintained it in print

parts.words: Thomas Fuller maintained it in print
parts.note: Thomas Fuller published a 1643 pamphlet titled '... Maintained', so the clue asks what he maintained

explanation.definitionFit: Fuller's 1643 work 'Truth Maintained' defended what he held to be fact against his critics.

clue.text: Orson Welles's Harry returns as äKastner's boy detective

indicators.note: returns means the surname is read backwards

parts.note: Welles played Harry Lime in The Third Man

explanation.surface: Welles's racketeer comes back as a German children's hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returns' turns LIME round. Erich Kästner's Emil and the Detectives (1929) has a boy who tracks down a thief in Berlin.
explanation.definitionFit: Emil Tischbein is the young hero who leads a gang of child sleuths in Kästner's novel.

clue.text: Remains of 14 heard in Marge Percy's paranoid Vida?

indicators.note: heard means the word for the residue is taken by its sound and spelt differently

parts.note: 14-down is about burning, and what remains after a fire is ash

explanation.surface: Burnt leftovers turn up in a novel about a paranoid fugitive.
explanation.walkthrough: Vida Asch is the hunted radical heroine of Marge Piercy's novel Vida (1979); the clue prints 'Percy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Vida Asch, the underground activist living in constant fear of arrest, gives Piercy's novel its title.

clue.text: Secular leaders of lost allegory in Comus

indicators.note: leaders of means the opening letter of each following word is taken

explanation.surface: Worldly leading figures in Milton's masque, a lost allegory.
explanation.walkthrough: Comus is Milton's masque; the allegory picture hides that only the initials count.
explanation.definitionFit: Lay, as opposed to clerical, means non-religious or secular.

clue.text: Composer of the old days in Belgium

definitions.meaning: Henri ... was a Belgian violinist and composer
in French, spoken in Belgium, the old days or times gone by

explanation.surface: A composer of yesteryear in Belgium.
explanation.definitionFit: The Belgian violinist-composer's surname is French for 'old time', fitting both senses.

clue.text: Her story was told by Patrick White, but it was with Greene she travelled

definitions.text: Her story was told by Patrick White, but it was with Greene she travelled

parts.words: Her story was told by Patrick White, but it was with Greene she travelled
parts.note: combines White's novel The ... Story with Greene's Travels with My ...

explanation.definitionFit: The relative appears in both titles: White's The Aunt's Story and Greene's Travels with My Aunt.

clue.text: Old fellow's family traced in Heinlein book

definitions.text: Old fellow's family traced in Heinlein book

parts.words: Old fellow's family traced in Heinlein book
parts.note: the old fellow is the longest-lived man in Genesis

explanation.definitionFit: The patriarch who lived 969 years is the archetypal old man, and Heinlein named his long-lived families after him.
